chapter_summary.text: This lesson focuses on reading skills and grammar strategies for the PTE Academic Re-order paragraphs item type. It covers identifying main ideas, supporting points, relationships between sentences and paragraphs, academic vocabulary, connotation and denotation, explicit and implicit information, concrete and abstract information, classifying and categorizing information, and following logical or chronological sequence.

evidence_spans.quote:
This lesson focuses on the following reading skills: 
• Identifying the topic, theme or main ideas
• Identifying supporting points or examples
• Identifying the relationship between sentences and paragraphs
• Understanding academic vocabulary
• Understanding the difference between connotation and denotation

• Comprehending explicit and implicit information 
• Comprehending concrete and abstract information
• Classifying and categorizing information
• Following a logical or chronological sequence of events
This lesson provides skills practice for the PTE Academic item type Re-order paragraphs.

core_lessons.title: Know What The Item Type Tests

explanation.text: The Re-order paragraphs item type tests your ability to understand the organization and cohesion of an academic text. The reading texts for this item are up to 150 words in length, and there are two to three items with such reading texts in PTE Academic.

core_lessons.title: Use Articles To Track New And Known Information

explanation.text: Indefinite articles are generally used when something is first introduced, while definite articles are used for later references to that thing, with superlatives, and when distinguishing one particular noun from similar nouns in the same class.

evidence_spans.quote: Indefinite articles are generally used when something is first introduced, with

definite articles used for subsequent references to that thing. Definite articles are also used when 
a specific noun is mentioned

Definite articles are also used with superlatives, e.g. ‘the tallest’, and when distinguishing 
one particular noun from other similar nouns in the same class

explanation.text: Pronouns and other referents help sequence sentences because they substitute for or refer to previously mentioned nouns. Singular countable nouns can be substituted with singular pronouns such as 'it', plural countable nouns with plural pronouns such as 'they', and specific or proper nouns with forms such as 'this' or 'that' plus a generic noun.

core_lessons.title: Use Discourse Markers To Recognize Relationships

explanation.text: Discourse markers signal relationships between ideas, including exemplifying, generalizing, joining or adding ideas, noting similarity, noting difference, cause and effect, sequencing stages or procedures, and summing up.

evidence_spans.quote:
Work in groups to match the language functions in the left hand column with the discourse markers 
in the right hand column.

Function Discourse markers
1. Exemplifying ‘for example’, ‘for instance’, ‘such as’
2. Generalizing ‘on the whole’, ‘by and large’, ‘basically’, ‘in general’

3. Joining or adding ideas ‘and’, ‘also’, ‘additionally’, ‘furthermore’, ‘moreover’, ‘as well’
4. Noting similarity ‘similarly’, ‘in the same way’, ‘likewise’

5. Noting difference ‘however’, ‘in contrast’, ‘on the other hand’, ‘though’, ‘nevertheless’
6. Signaling cause and effect ‘therefore’, ‘so’, ‘as a consequence’, ‘consequently’, ‘as a result’, ‘thus’

7. Sequencing stages or 
procedures ‘first’, ‘secondly’, ‘finally’, ‘lastly’, ‘after this’, ‘then’
8. Summing up ‘in short’, ‘in conclusion’

worked_examples.title: Article Clues In A Burj Dubai Paragraph

example.text: Try ordering these sentence ideas: first introduce the Burj Dubai, then describe the height of the building, then explain the word 'estimated', then introduce a hotel in the building, and finally use 'that' to refer back to the hotel.

explanation.text: The source answer key orders the Burj Dubai paragraph by first identifying the topic sentence, then using 'the building' to refer to the Burj Dubai, 'the use of the ...' to refer to statistics in the previous sentence, 'A hotel' to introduce new information, and 'that' to refer to the hotel.

evidence_spans.quote:
One of the world’s tallest structures is the Burj Dubai. (This is the topic sentence because it introduces the 
paragraph’s main topic: The Burj Dubai.)

Standing at 167 floors, the height of the building is widely estimated to be 707 metres. (The words ‘the 
building’ refer to the Burj Dubai.)

Note the use of the qualifier “estimated”; the building’s exact height is a tightly guarded secret. (The phrase 
‘the use of the …’ refers to the statistics in the previous sentence
A hotel occupies the bottom 37 floors of the building. (‘A hotel’ introduces new information

Above that, on floors 45 through 108 are apartments and corporate offices. (The word ‘that’ refers to the 
hotel.)

worked_examples.title: Referent Clues In A Valentine's Day Paragraph

example.text: When a sentence says 'The holiday', look backward for the named holiday. When a sentence says 'this pagan festival', look backward for the festival just introduced. When a sentence says 'this early Pope', look backward for the Pope just named.

explanation.text: The source answer key shows that 'The holiday' refers to Valentine's Day, 'This pagan festival' refers to the fertility celebration in the previous sentence, and 'this early Pope' refers to Pope Gelasius I.

evidence_spans.quote:
The holiday’s roots are in the ancient Roman festival of Lupercalia, a fertility celebration commemorated annually 
on February 15. (‘The holiday’ refers to Valentine’s Day.)

Pope Gelasius I recast this pagan festival as a Christian feast day circa 496, declaring February 14 to be St. 
Valentine’s Day. (‘This pagan festival’ refers to ‘a fertility celebration commemorated annually on 
February 15’

Which St. Valentine this early Pope intended to honor remains a mystery: according to the Catholic Encyclopedia, 
there were at least three early Christian saints by that name. (The phrase ‘this early Pope’ refers to Pope 
Gelasius I

misconception.text: Any sentence that contains a definite article can safely begin a Re-order paragraphs item.

correction.text: A definite article can depend on information in a previous sentence, while an indefinite article can mark the first reference to the item type.

evidence_spans.quote:
The indefinite article (‘a reading item 
type’) is used in this sentence because it is the first reference to the item type.

The definite article in the second sentence (‘The item type’) depends on the information in the previous sentence to make 
sense.

misconception.text: Pronouns can be interpreted without checking earlier sentences.

correction.text: Pronouns and reference phrases can depend on backward reference to nouns or noun phrases in previous sentences.

evidence_spans.quote: The use of the reference pronoun (‘for this item’) depends on the information in the previous sentence to make sense.

The use of the pronoun (‘such reading texts’) depends on the backwards reference to the noun phrase ‘reading texts’ in the 
previous sentence to make sense.

The use of the pronoun (‘They’) depends on the backwards reference to the noun phrase ‘two to three items with such 
reading texts’ in the previous sentence to make sense.

question.text: You see five jumbled sentences. What should you identify first before ordering the remaining supporting sentences?

answer.text: Identify the topic sentence first, then use clues such as articles, referents, and discourse markers to order the supporting sentences.

question.text: In a paragraph, why might 'the building' be unlikely to appear before the building has been introduced?

answer.text: Because a definite article often points back to something already introduced. A first mention is more likely to use an indefinite article or name the noun directly.

question.text: Match the discourse marker function to an example: cause and effect; contrast; summing up. Use examples from this chapter.

answer.text: Cause and effect: 'therefore', 'so', 'as a result', or 'thus'. Contrast: 'however', 'in contrast', 'on the other hand', 'though', or 'nevertheless'. Summing up: 'in short' or 'in conclusion'.

question.text: If a sentence begins with 'They', what should you look for in earlier sentences?

answer.text: Look for a previous plural noun or noun phrase that 'They' can refer back to.

review_checklist.text: I can identify a topic sentence before ordering supporting sentences.
I can use definite and indefinite articles to track first mention and later reference.
I can use pronouns and other referents to connect a sentence to information in a previous sentence.
I can recognize discourse markers for addition, contrast, similarity, cause and effect, sequencing, examples, generalization, and conclusion.
I can practise Re-order paragraphs quickly while remembering that the Reading items are not timed individually.
